newsitem.title: ALBANIA: EU readies aid effort to Albania backed by troops.
newsitem.headline: EU readies aid effort to Albania backed by troops.

text.p: France flew 40 tonnes of humanitarian aid to Albania on Tuesday as Europe prepared to launch a major relief effort for the stricken country backed by troops to help it get through if necessary.

European Union foreign ministers said on Monday they would not object to individual countries sending troops to protect aid convoys, but for the second time in eight days backed away from organising their own multinational force.

Hans van Mierlo, Dutch Foreign Minister and current EU president, said a "coalition of the willing" existed, with countries inside and outside the bloc prepared to send troops if necessary. Turkey has already made clear it is among them.
Italian television reported that Italy, France, Spain and Portugal were expected to provide forces to any security operation, with Greece, Romania and Hungary contributing at a later stage.

The need for some sort of outside armed force to protect aid convoys from gunmen who rule parts of the country after looting thousands of weapons from army depots was graphically underlined by the killing of four policemen in Albania during the night.

Police said three of the policemen were killed in the rebel-held southern port of Vlore in an apparent ambush by criminal gangs late on Monday night. Gunmen in two cars blocked their way as they were chasing a suspected stolen car and shot them with automatic weapons. Another policemen was killed in Tirana.

French military planes flew into Tirana airport, only a day after it reopened for scheduled flights after being closed for 11 days by the armed turmoil in the country, bringing 40 tonnes of sugar, flour, pasta, milk powder and medicine.

The EU estimates that basic medical supplies and 10,000 tonnes of flour are urgently needed by Albania, ravaged by an armed rebellion in the south over failed savings schemes that quickly spread unrest to the north.
Italy has already flown two tonnes of emergency medical aid to the rebel-held south and six tonnes to Tirana in the government-controlled north.

At the Adriatic port of Durres, some 40 kms (25 miles) west of Tirana, the situation was reported by port officials to be calm on Tuesday after Italian and Albanian leaders acted to stem a flood of refugees fleeing to Italy.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said after talks with Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Monday they had agreed to conduct naval patrols in the Adriatic to halt the flow. Nearly 12,000 have fled since March 13.

Prodi did not make clear whether Italian ships would enter Albanian territorial waters, though military sources said the Navy was already carrying out orders to intercept Albanian boats and advise them to turn back for home.

The operation follows mounting evidence that recent arrivals were no longer genuine refugees but illegal immigrants looking for a better life who had paid Albanian mafias money for a passage, Italian officials said.
Fino, who heads a national unity government installed in response to the armed anarchy, said on Monday he wanted Albanians to remain and help rebuild the country.
"We agree that Italy should patrol the entire Adriatic to stop this exodus because Albania's problems have to be resolved by the Albanians themselves in Albania," Fino said.
He said international relief aid was a crucial element in any attempt to stem the exodus. "That is the only way to give Albanians faith in this government's ability to govern."
